summary: An informational memo that grew from a deposition submitted in a challenge to the Communications Decency Act of 1996. It discusses access control on the Internet and whether it is feasible.

plainLanguage.summary: This note comes from a court case about internet rules, and talks about how access to things can be controlled.

questions: communications decency act and internet access control
why is age verification impossible on the internet
can servers control who sees their content
subtitle: Why content filtering by the sender is technically impractical on the Internet

tldr.problem: The Communications Decency Act of 1996 required senders of potentially offensive content to take effective action to prevent minors from seeing it, but the Internet's distributed architecture makes this technically infeasible for most communication methods.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC examines major Internet communication channels—from email to USENET to the Web—and demonstrates that senders and servers lack the technical ability to verify recipients' ages or prevent minors from accessing content in each case.
tldr.outcome: The document argues that the only practical approach to content control is client-side filtering installed on individual computers, not server-side or sender-side restriction.

today: RFC 2057 is Informational and reflects the state of the Internet in 1996. The technical arguments about internet decentralization remain largely valid, though methods for age verification and content blocking have evolved. The RFC remains relevant for understanding why server-side content control at scale is technically impractical.

sections.title: The Technical Challenge of the Communications Decency Act
sections.content:
This RFC was submitted as expert testimony in a legal challenge to the Communications Decency Act of 1996, which required senders of potentially offensive material to take "effective action" to prevent minors from accessing it. The author examines whether this requirement is technically feasible given how the Internet actually works.

The Internet is not a centralized system that any single authority can control. Instead, it consists of millions of computers owned by countless independent organizations, connected by thousands of service providers. This fundamental decentralization means that neither the sender nor the server can reliably know who will ultimately receive a message or verify their age.
sections.plainLanguage: The government wanted internet companies to stop kids from seeing adult stuff, but the internet is too spread out and chaotic for that to actually work the way they imagined.

sections.title: Why Nobody Controls the Internet
sections.content:
No single organization operates or controls the Internet. Although standards-setting bodies like the IETF, IAB, ISOC, and IESG develop protocols and define how the Internet works, none of them controls the content flowing through it or can require providers to restrict access.

The only centralized functions are the allocation of IP addresses (handled by InterNIC and regional partners) and domain name registration. Even these do not give anyone the power to control content. Worse, IP address allocation is unreliable: many users receive dynamic IP addresses that change between sessions, and addresses can be translated by firewalls, making the source address an unreliable identifier of the user.
sections.plainLanguage: The people who make internet rules do not run the internet. Each computer owner controls their own computer, and there is no central database of who is using what address.

sections.title: Point-to-Point Communications: Email
sections.content:
For email between two parties, a sender might personally know the recipient and thus be relatively confident they are an adult. But when an email sender does not know the recipient, age verification becomes extremely difficult.

Email addresses provide no authoritative information about the addressee. Addresses are self-chosen and often not based on real names. There is no universal directory of email addresses with corresponding ages. Creating such a directory would be incomplete, unreliable, and likely out of date. Users can easily create aliases and temporary addresses, or use anonymous remailers that strip the original sender's address. Even if a sender could somehow verify that an email address belongs to an adult, they cannot be sure that the adult is not sharing their account with a minor.
sections.plainLanguage: With email, you cannot tell who is on the other end. They can claim any name, and even if you verify one person, someone else might be reading their email.

sections.title: Point-to-Multipoint Communications: Mailing Lists and Newsgroups
sections.content:
When one sender posts to a mailing list, the message goes to everyone on that list. The sender typically has no way to know who is subscribed, let alone their ages. They cannot restrict access to specific individuals. Some mailing lists are moderated, but even then, the moderator cannot control final distribution. Mailing lists can subscribe other mailing lists, causing messages to re-explode to entirely separate lists beyond the original sender's knowledge.

USENET newsgroups are even more distributed. When a message is posted, it propagates automatically to thousands of servers worldwide with no central control. The original poster has no ability to monitor or control who reads it. New servers can join the distribution system at any time, and the poster will not even know they exist. Different servers can be configured to carry different newsgroups, and there is no mechanism to restrict distribution based on individual message content.
sections.plainLanguage: When you post to a mailing list or newsgroup, your message bounces around to thousands of computers, and you have no idea who ends up reading it.

sections.title: Information Retrieval Systems: From FTP to the Web
sections.content:
In anonymous FTP, users enter "anonymous" as the username and can browse shared files. While users might enter an email address as the password, there is no validation: the FTP server has no way to verify the user's identity or age. Non-anonymous FTP requires individual accounts, which creates administrative burden and security risks.

Gopher servers have no built-in screening mechanism at all. The World Wide Web is the most capable of these: servers can use HTML forms and CGI scripts to interrogate visitors and grant or deny access. However, three major obstacles exist: (1) many Web publishers cannot run CGI scripts (such as those hosted on AOL or CompuServe), (2) Web page caching on the Internet causes content to be served from intermediate caches, bypassing the original server's screening, and (3) the administrative burden of verifying and managing access for thousands of daily visitors is enormous.
sections.plainLanguage: FTP and Gopher have no way to check ages at all. Websites can try to check, but caches spread their content everywhere, and many website hosts are not allowed to run the screening software.

sections.title: Client-Side Filtering as the Only Practical Solution
sections.content:
Given the infeasibility of sender or server-side screening, the most effective approach is client-side filtering—software installed on individual users' computers that blocks unwanted content. Such software can use content tags or third-party ratings to determine what users see.

The RFC notes that even tagging proposed by government would be ineffective: browsers would need to be configured to recognize and block tagged content, but senders have no way to ensure that happens. Also, many documents (executable programs, binary files) cannot be tagged without rendering them useless. Regardless, most Internet communication requires affirmative action by the listener—a person must choose to retrieve email, join a newsgroup, or visit a website. These are not passive communications that invade the home unbidden.
sections.plainLanguage: The only thing that actually works is software on your computer at home that parents can set up to block things they do not want kids to see. It cannot work if the server tries to check.
